marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q015.takeaway: At the elbow, ulnar injury paralyzes all palmar and dorsal interossei; medial FDP is also affected, but complete FDP paralysis is not expected.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q015.displayText: Paralysis of all interossei is seen in ulnar nerve injury at the elbow. All dorsal and palmar interossei are ulnar supplied: dorsal interossei abduct (DAB) and palmar interossei adduct (PAD). Combined median and ulnar injury can lead to total claw hand.
emphasis: Paralysis of all interossei is seen in ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
All dorsal and palmar interossei are ulnar supplied: dorsal interossei abduct (DAB) and palmar interossei adduct (PAD)
Combined median and ulnar injury can lead to total claw hand

rationales.a: Total claw hand generally requires combined median and ulnar intrinsic denervation.
rationales.c: Only the medial half of FDP is ulnar-innervated; the lateral half retains median/AIN supply.
rationales.d: The lateral two lumbricals are median-innervated and therefore are not all paralyzed by ulnar injury.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q016.takeaway: The thumb permits separate bedside tests of median opposition, ulnar adduction and radial extension/abduction.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q016.displayText: The thumb can be used to test radial, ulnar and median nerve function. Median nerve: opponens pollicis, tested by thumb opposition. Ulnar nerve: adductor pollicis/palmar interossei, tested by thumb adduction. Radial nerve: abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis longus, tested by thumb extension.
emphasis: The thumb can be used to test radial, ulnar and median nerve function
Median nerve: opponens pollicis, tested by thumb opposition
Ulnar nerve: adductor pollicis/palmar interossei, tested by thumb adduction

rationales.a: The ring finger does not provide this three-nerve combination of distinctive thumb actions.
rationales.b: Index finger function is useful for selected median testing but does not test all three nerves as directly as thumb maneuvers.
rationales.c: Little-finger movement mainly assesses ulnar function, not median and radial function together.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q017.takeaway: The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of arm is a radial-nerve branch, so its sensory territory maps to the radial nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q017.displayText: The lower lateral part of the arm is supplied by the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, one of the radial-nerve branches arising in the spiral groove. The radial nerve is the largest brachial-plexus branch (C5-T1), leaves the axilla through the lower triangular space, travels in the radial groove with profunda brachii, and gives lower lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm, branches to lateral and medial heads of triceps, and branch to anconeus. At the cubital fossa it divides into superficial sensory and deep motor branches; the deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve traverses supinator and supplies forearm extensors.
emphasis: The lower lateral part of the arm is supplied by the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, one of the radial-nerve branches arising in the spiral groove

The radial nerve is the largest brachial-plexus branch (C5-T1), leaves the axilla through the lower triangular space, travels in the radial groove with profunda brachii, and gives lower lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm, branches to lateral and medial heads of triceps, and branch to anconeus
At the cubital fossa it divides into superficial sensory and deep motor branches; the deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve traverses supinator and supplies forearm extensors

rationales.a: Axillary cutaneous supply is mainly the upper lateral cutaneous nerve over the deltoid badge area.
rationales.c: Median nerve does not supply the lower lateral arm skin.
rationales.d: Ulnar cutaneous territories are medial hand/forearm rather than lower lateral arm.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q018.takeaway: Radial-head fracture with finger MCP-extension weakness but preserved wrist extension and sensation suggests posterior interosseous motor neuropathy.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q018.displayText: The presentation indicates posterior interosseous nerve injury. It is vulnerable in radial-head/neck fractures because the nerve winds around the radial neck into the posterior forearm. Lesions confined to the posterior interosseous nerve cause no cutaneous sensory loss. The deep radial branch supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis and supinator, then continues as the posterior interosseous nerve and passes near the supinator arch/arcade of Frohse.
emphasis: The presentation indicates posterior interosseous nerve injury
It is vulnerable in radial-head/neck fractures because the nerve winds around the radial neck into the posterior forearm
Lesions confined to the posterior interosseous nerve cause no cutaneous sensory loss

rationales.a: A lesion of the radial trunk below the spiral groove would more broadly weaken wrist/finger extension and may affect cutaneous branches.
rationales.b: Anterior interosseous nerve is a median motor branch to deep flexors, not finger extensors.
rationales.d: Common extensor-origin injury would not selectively explain the nerve-pattern weakness associated with radial-head trauma.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q019.takeaway: C6–C7 root involvement affects thumb and index-finger sensation in the source dermatome mapping.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q019.displayText: With C6 and C7 root injury, sensation over the thumb and index finger is lost. The palmar pad of the thumb is supplied by C6 and the pad of the index finger by C7.
emphasis: With C6 and C7 root injury, sensation over the thumb and index finger is lost
The palmar pad of the thumb is supplied by C6 and the pad of the index finger by C7

rationales.b: Little-finger sensation maps chiefly to C8.
rationales.c: The upper medial arm is supplied from upper thoracic/medial cutaneous distributions, not C6–C7.
rationales.d: The medial forearm is mainly T1 via the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q020.takeaway: The triceps tendon reflex predominantly tests C7; the biceps reflex predominantly tests C6.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q020.displayText: Tapping the triceps tendon posterior to the elbow predominantly tests C7. Tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa predominantly tests C6.
emphasis: Tapping the triceps tendon posterior to the elbow predominantly tests C7
Tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa predominantly tests C6

rationales.a: C6 is the main biceps-reflex segment, not triceps.
rationales.c: C5 is proximal to the principal triceps-reflex level.
rationales.d: C8 is not the predominant triceps reflex segment.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q021.takeaway: A lower spiral-groove radial lesion may interrupt the lateral-head triceps branch, which arises at that level.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q021.displayText: The lateral head of triceps may be paralyzed in a lower radial-groove lesion because its branch arises in the lower spiral groove. Anconeus receives a branch from the spiral groove. The radial nerve is a posterior-cord branch, exits the axilla through the lower triangular space, and in the arm travels in the radial groove with the profunda brachii artery, not the brachial artery.
emphasis: The lateral head of triceps may be paralyzed in a lower radial-groove lesion because its branch arises in the lower spiral groove
Anconeus receives a branch from the spiral groove
The radial nerve is a posterior-cord branch, exits the axilla through the lower triangular space, and in the arm travels in the radial groove with the profunda brachii artery, not the brachial artery

rationales.a: The radial nerve exits the axilla through the lower triangular space, not quadrangular space.
rationales.c: The anconeus branch arises in the spiral groove, rather than in the axilla.
rationales.d: In the arm the radial nerve accompanies profunda brachii in the radial groove, not the brachial artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q022.takeaway: Thenar eminence skin is usually spared in carpal tunnel syndrome because the palmar cutaneous median branch leaves proximal to the flexor retinaculum.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q022.displayText: Paresthesia over the skin of the thenar eminence is not prominent in carpal tunnel syndrome because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before it enters the tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome may result from reduced tunnel size, flexor-tendon synovial thickening/tenosynovitis, inflammation of the flexor retinaculum, or arthritic carpal changes including rheumatoid arthritis. Pain and paresthesia are often worse at night and with gripping. Contents include FDS, FDP and FPL tendons plus median nerve; no artery passes through the tunnel.
emphasis: Paresthesia over the skin of the thenar eminence is not prominent in carpal tunnel syndrome because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before it enters the tunnel

Carpal tunnel syndrome may result from reduced tunnel size, flexor-tendon synovial thickening/tenosynovitis, inflammation of the flexor retinaculum, or arthritic carpal changes including rheumatoid arthritis
Pain and paresthesia are often worse at night and with gripping

rationales.a: Rheumatoid synovial changes can narrow the tunnel and cause median compression.
rationales.b: Night-worsening pain and paresthesia are common in carpal tunnel syndrome.
rationales.d: The source lists tendons and median nerve as tunnel contents and no artery passes through it.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q023.takeaway: A deep radial-sided wrist slash can injure radial artery and flexor-side structures, but the radial nerve is not the likely structure at that site.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q023.displayText: A deep radial-side wrist laceration may injure the radial artery, median nerve, flexor carpi radialis tendon and palmaris longus tendon. The radial nerve is therefore least likely to be injured. A deep ulnar-side laceration may injure ulnar artery, ulnar nerve and flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.
emphasis: A deep radial-side wrist laceration may injure the radial artery, median nerve, flexor carpi radialis tendon and palmaris longus tendon
The radial nerve is therefore least likely to be injured
A deep ulnar-side laceration may injure ulnar artery, ulnar nerve and flexor carpi ulnaris tendon

rationales.a: The radial artery is exposed on the radial side of the wrist.
rationales.c: Flexor carpi radialis tendon lies at the radial wrist and can be cut.
rationales.d: Palmaris longus tendon is a superficial volar wrist structure that may also be injured.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q024.takeaway: Guyon canal roof is the palmar carpal ligament with palmaris brevis; its contents are ulnar nerve and artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q024.displayText: The marked structure is Guyon's canal. Its roof is formed by the palmar carpal ligament and palmaris brevis. The source describes the canal as a roughly 4-cm canal along the anteromedial wrist. Boundaries: medial/ulnar side - pisiform, flexor carpi ulnaris and abductor digiti minimi; lateral side - hook of hamate, extrinsic flexor tendons and transverse carpal ligament; floor - flexor retinaculum and pisohamate ligaments; roof - palmar carpal ligament and palmaris brevis. Contents are ulnar nerve and ulnar artery.
emphasis: The marked structure is Guyon's canal
Its roof is formed by the palmar carpal ligament and palmaris brevis
The source describes the canal as a roughly 4-cm canal along the anteromedial wrist

rationales.a: Pisiform, FCU and abductor digiti minimi define the medial boundary, not the roof.
rationales.b: Flexor retinaculum and pisohamate ligaments form the floor.
rationales.c: Hook of hamate, flexor tendons and transverse carpal ligament form the lateral boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q025.takeaway: Ulnar injury at the medial epicondyle does not completely paralyze digits three and four because median and radial extrinsic tendons still flex and extend them.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q025.displayText: Medial epicondyle injury damages the ulnar nerve. Complete paralysis of the third and fourth digits is least likely because flexor digitorum superficialis (median nerve) and extensor digitorum (radial nerve) remain functional. Ulnar injury can weaken flexor carpi ulnaris causing reduced ulnar deviation/flexion, paralyze medial FDP, produce hypothenar atrophy, and reduce sensation over the medial hand/medial 1½ fingers.
emphasis: Medial epicondyle injury damages the ulnar nerve
Complete paralysis of the third and fourth digits is least likely because flexor digitorum superficialis (median nerve) and extensor digitorum (radial nerve) remain functional
Ulnar injury can weaken flexor carpi ulnaris causing reduced ulnar deviation/flexion, paralyze medial FDP, produce hypothenar atrophy, and reduce sensation over the medial hand/medial 1½ fingers

rationales.a: FCU weakness can reduce wrist flexion and ulnar deviation after ulnar injury.
rationales.c: Hypothenar atrophy follows denervation of ulnar intrinsic muscles.
rationales.d: Reduced sensation over the hypothenar eminence is consistent with ulnar sensory loss.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q026.takeaway: Long thoracic nerve integrity is tested by asking the patient to elevate the arm above the head, requiring serratus anterior upward rotation.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q026.displayText: Long thoracic nerve injury during radical mastectomy paralyzes serratus anterior. Integrity is tested by asking the patient to raise the arm above the head on the affected side. Shoulder shrug primarily tests trapezius/spinal accessory nerve, while touching the opposite shoulder involves pectoralis major supplied mainly by medial and lateral pectoral nerves.
emphasis: Long thoracic nerve injury during radical mastectomy paralyzes serratus anterior

Shoulder shrug primarily tests trapezius/spinal accessory nerve, while touching the opposite shoulder involves pectoralis major supplied mainly by medial and lateral pectoral nerves

rationales.a: Shoulder shrug tests trapezius and spinal accessory nerve.
rationales.c: Touching the opposite shoulder primarily engages pectoralis major and shoulder adduction.
rationales.d: Lifting a heavy object is not the specific serratus-anterior test described.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q027.takeaway: The anterior axial line extends from the sternal-angle region down to the wrist; the posterior axial line reaches the elbow.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q027.displayText: The anterior axial line extends to the wrist joint. An axial line is a junction between dermatomes supplied by discontinuous spinal nerves. The anterior axial line starts near the sternal angle/second rib and extends to the wrist; the posterior axial line begins at the shoulder and reaches the elbow.
emphasis: The anterior axial line extends to the wrist joint
An axial line is a junction between dermatomes supplied by discontinuous spinal nerves
The anterior axial line starts near the sternal angle/second rib and extends to the wrist; the posterior axial line begins at the shoulder and reaches the elbow

rationales.a: Shoulder marks the proximal origin region, not the distal endpoint of the anterior line.
rationales.b: Elbow is the endpoint described for the posterior axial line.
rationales.d: The anterior line extends farther distally to the wrist joint.

marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q028.takeaway: Main en griffe combines MCP hyperextension with IP flexion after loss of lumbrical/interosseous balance.
marrow__ANAT_CH38_Q028.displayText: Main en griffe (claw hand) consists of extension/hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints due to ulnar nerve injury. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, which normally flex MCP joints and extend IP joints. Loss of their action leaves extensor digitorum and long finger flexors unopposed.
emphasis: Main en griffe (claw hand) consists of extension/hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints due to ulnar nerve injury
The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, which normally flex MCP joints and extend IP joints
Loss of their action leaves extensor digitorum and long finger flexors unopposed

rationales.b: Clawing features MCP extension with IP flexion, not extension at both joint levels.
rationales.c: Both-joint flexion does not describe classic ulnar clawing.
rationales.d: MCP flexion with IP extension is the intrinsic-plus pattern, opposite of claw hand.
